turns.question: What are you studying or working on right now, and what part of it takes most of your week?
turns.answer: I'm still working as a hospice nurse, so most of my week is patient visits and families. I see several people a week at their homes or in facility rooms, and a lot of the time goes to the families more than the patients, honestly. Some weeks it's mostly driving between visits and charting afterward, but the part that takes the most out of me is the conversations where someone's just learned the time is short.

turns.question: Think of one of those conversations that has stayed with you most. What did the room look like when you walked in?
turns.answer: I can think of one from a few years back. A man in his seventies, his wife and their two grown daughters were in the front room, and the TV was on with the sound off. The daughters had clearly been told something vague by the doctor already, because they kept saying "he's not doing well" and looking at each other. The wife was holding a mug of coffee that had gone cold. There was a recliner, a couple of kitchen chairs, and nobody was sitting in the chairs. Everyone was standing near the door like they wanted to be able to leave.

turns.question: In that front room, what was the first thing you said, and to whom did you say it?
turns.answer: I sat down in one of the kitchen chairs first, which pulled everyone's attention over to me. Then I looked at the wife, since she was the one who'd be the most affected, and I said that he was dying. Just that, plainly, with the word dying in it. The daughters went very still. I didn't say anything else right away. I just stayed quiet for a bit and let it land, because I've learned that if I rush to fill the silence, people get lost in what I'm saying instead of what's happening to them.

turns.question: What do newer nurses usually do in the first minute of a room like that one that you've had to unlearn?
turns.answer:
Mostly they try to explain too fast. They stand there with the chart or the pamphlet and start walking the family through what's coming, because the silence feels like something they have to fix. I did that too when I started out, back in the ICU days when I was used to giving people a lot of information quickly.

What I've had to unlearn is the idea that my job in that first minute is to say something smart. It's really to say the true thing and then get out of the way. A lot of the mentoring I do with new grads is just getting them to sit down, say the word, and then count to ten in their head before they open their mouth again. Most of them are terrified of that silence, and I understand why, but the families usually need it more than they need an explanation.

turns.question: Think of the point when you moved from the ICU toward hospice work. What was the moment you decided, and what were you doing right before it?
turns.answer:
I don't think there was one single moment, honestly. It was more of a slow build. In the ICU we were so focused on keeping people alive, and that's not a bad thing, but I kept noticing how little time anyone spent on how the dying actually went. I was on a night shift, sitting at the station after a long code, and I just thought, I don't want my whole career to be about the machines. That was the closest thing to a decision I had.

Then I applied to a hospice and it took a while to get in, and honestly the first few months I doubted myself. I missed the adrenaline a little. But I'm glad I made the switch.

turns.question: Think of the last new grad you sat with after a hard visit. What was the first thing they did in a room that told you they'd be all right?
turns.answer:
Honestly, it was the sitting down. There was a young woman I mentored last spring, her first month on the job. We got to a house where the family was standing by the door, and instead of staying on her feet she pulled a chair over and sat, and then she said the word dying before anything else. She didn't dress it up. I could see her hands were shaking a little, but she stayed put.

What told me she'd be fine was that after she said it, she didn't rush. She let the quiet sit there, even though I could tell it was uncomfortable for her. Most new grads want to fill that gap with information, so seeing her hold still was a relief.

turns.question: Outside of patients and charting, what do you spend time on that has nothing to do with nursing?
turns.answer: I garden, mostly tomatoes and whatever the rabbits haven't gotten to yet. My husband says I talk to the plants more than I talk to him, which is probably true after a long week. On Sundays I try to walk the lake path near my house if the weather cooperates, and I read mysteries, the cozy kind, because I want something where everyone gets sorted out by the last page.

turns.question: You said the chair first, then the word. Think of the first time you watched a new grad sit down and then rush anyway. What did she do in the next thirty seconds?
turns.answer:
Honestly I don't think I've seen that happen with a new grad in a way I'd want to describe to someone. Most of them sit down and say the word, and then the rushing comes after, and it's usually me who sees it, not them. But I can tell you what it usually looks like. Their eyes go to the chart or the pamphlet on their knee, and they start in on the next steps, like how the hospice team will come out, what the medications do, what to expect over the next few days. Somewhere in there the wife or one of the daughters stops looking at them and starts looking at the floor.

When I see that, I usually just lean forward a little and say the person's name, or ask the family what's been hardest today. That tends to bring them back into the room. It's not a big thing to do, but it helps.

turns.question: When families are standing by the door, what is it they most need a nurse to know before anything gets explained?
turns.answer: I think they need to know that someone is willing to stay in the room with them. Explanations can wait. Most families are so scared that they can't take in much of what gets said anyway, so if the first thing they hear is a clear, true sentence and then a little quiet, they start to trust that you're not going to run past what's happening to them.

turns.question: While the hospice was still deciding on you, what did you do with those months?
turns.answer: I don't think I did anything dramatic with them. I was working a few shifts a week at the hospital still, so I kept at that and tried not to overthink the application. The waiting was the hard part. I kept second-guessing whether I was just running from the ICU or actually going somewhere. I spent a lot of time in the garden that spring, which helped more than I expected.

turns.question: What do new grads come to you for that they wouldn't think to ask about?
turns.answer: Honestly, I think they come to me for permission more than information. They want to know if it's okay to sit down when everyone else is standing, or if it's okay to say the word "dying" out loud. Most of them were taught to be careful with that word, and they worry that saying it plainly will hurt someone. They don't usually think to ask how to handle the silence afterward, but that's the part that trips them up most.

turns.question: You said you kept asking whether you were running from the ICU or actually going somewhere. What was one test you used to tell the difference?
turns.answer: I don't know that I had a real test, honestly. I think I just kept asking myself a simple question on the bad shifts: when I pictured the next week, was I picturing a room where I was helping someone die well, or was I picturing getting away from the monitors? Most days the honest answer was the first one, even when I was tired. That was about as scientific as I got.

turns.question: When a new grad has just sat through a hard visit like that, what do you say to them in the car afterward?
turns.answer:
Usually I ask them how they're doing, and I mean that as a real question, not a formality. Most of them go quiet for a minute, and I let them. Then I'll often ask what the family said that stuck with them, or what they wish they'd done differently. Sometimes they want to talk through it and sometimes they just want the radio on, and I try to notice which.

If they're beating themselves up about the silence, I tell them that sitting there was the job, even if it felt like nothing was happening. They don't have to have said the right thing. They only had to stay in the room.

turns.question: You said the hospice took a while to take you. When they asked why you wanted to leave the ICU, what did you actually say, and what did you leave out?
turns.answer: I told them what I've told you, more or less: that I wanted to spend my time on how people die, not just on keeping them alive. That part was true. The part I left out was that I'd been feeling burned out for a while and wasn't sure I could keep doing ICU nights much longer. I didn't see the point of making that the headline in an interview. I figured they'd see it soon enough if I was any good at the work, and I was honest with myself about it even if I didn't say it to them.

turns.question: Is this you? You sit down before you speak, say the word dying plainly, then hold the quiet so families can trust you. You teach new grads to get past that silence, including the car ride after a hard visit. And you left the ICU by asking which room you were picturing for next week.
turns.answer:
Yes, that's me, mostly. The sitting down and the word dying, I'd stand by. The quiet I'd put a little differently, though. I don't think of it as holding the quiet so they'll trust me. It's more that the quiet is when they get to catch up to what's happening, and I'm just trying not to get in the way of that.

On the car rides, I'd push back a little on "get past" the silence. I don't tell them to get past it. I tell them the silence was the job, and then I ask how they're doing and mean it.

The ICU part is a bit simplified. I didn't really leave on one clean question. It was more that on the bad shifts I kept asking myself which room I was picturing, and most days it was the hospice one. That's about as tidy as it gets.
turns.playback: You sit down before you speak, say the word dying plainly, then hold the quiet so families can trust you. You teach new grads to get past that silence, including the car ride after a hard visit. And you left the ICU by asking which room you were picturing for next week.

turns.question: Is that the version you'd put in the book?
turns.answer: Yeah, that's close. I'd maybe say it a bit plainer than that, though. I don't think there's a version for a book. It's just what I keep telling the new ones, usually while we're both trying to get the car started. If someone wrote it down, I'd want them to include that the chair part matters more than people think, and that nobody gets it right the first few times.
turns.playback: The sitting down and saying dying plainly come first, and then the quiet is when families get to catch up to what's happening. With new grads in the car, the silence was the job, and then you ask how they're doing and mean it.
